newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries close higher following FOMC vote.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries close higher following FOMC vote.

text.p: U.S. Treasury securities prices closed on a firm note -- especially at the short end -- after the Federal Reserve's policy-making arm announced it would not raise short-term interest rates on Tuesday.
The Federal Open Market Committee voted to leave monetary policy unchanged at its meeting, causing a sharp runup in short-term rates and volatility at the long end of the maturity spectrum.
The dollar fell sharply after the decision was announced, dropping below key levels, traders said.

Analysts had been divided as whether the Fed would vote to tighten interest rates as no overt signs of inflationary pressure had been seen in recent economic reports. Weaker retail sales were seen last month and Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan had stated he would look for a slackening economy rather than strong inflationary signals in deciding whether to further tighten short-term interest rates.

The Fed, under Greenspan's tutelage has never moved only only once to tighten or ease. However, economists said the spread between real interest rates and federal funds was not as wide as it was in 1994 -- the Fed's last tightening cycle.
"We're seeing the short end outperform the long end, as it should," said Kathy Bostjancic, economist at UBS Securities Inc. "We still have the bears and the bulls wrestling each other."
"We'll have to continue to monitor the economic numbers. Our official forecast is that they go (tighten) again in July" but the state of the economy had to watched, she said.

"I guessed the odds were 55 percent to 45 percent they would raise" the federal funds rate, said Paul Samuelson, economics professor and Nobel Prize winner at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Samuelson said a cost/benefit calculation leaned in favor of the Fed tightening. "They're running the risk toward inflation," he said.
Samuelson said it was not a given that the Fed would tighten in July. "They have another bite at the apple, but it could be a standoff," he said.
Samuelson the U.S. economy was doing very well compared with other major economies. He attributed much of that to the labor market.
"People are accepting jobs that aren't necessarily good, but they are available," he said.
In countries such as France, workers had very strong union representation, making it difficult for companies to downsize, Samuelson said.

As expected, there was a flurry of trading following release of the Fed's decision. Between 1415 EDT/1815 GMT and 1500 EDT/1900 GMT some $18.6 billion in Treasuries traded, said Maureen Mooney, senior analyst at GovPX.
Some $2.8 billion of the activity was in two-year notes and some $3.5 billion in three-month bills -- almost triple the normal volume, Mooney said.
The 30-year bond was up 7/32 at 96-16 to yield 6.90 percent. The 10-year note closed at 99-20/32, up 8/32 to yield 6.68 percent. Five-year notes ended at 100-15/32, up 7/32 to yield 6.51 percent.
Near the shorter end of the maturity range, two-year notes closed at 100-10/32, up 4/32 to yield 6.20 percent.
Three-month bill rates fell nine basis points to 5.08 percent. Six-month bill rates fell 13 basis points to 5.27 percent. Year bill rates fell eight basis points to 5.47 percent.
